title: Right upper quadrant pain, fever and yellow skin in a 28-year-old teacher
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 28-year-old school teacher in a rural ED. She has had fevers since last night and 2 hours of severe crampy right upper quadrant pain, her husband has noticed yellow skin, and she has rigors, pale stools, dark urine and itch. The candidate then interprets her observations, blood results with a venous gas and an upper abdominal ultrasound report. They give the diagnosis and differentials, outline sepsis management and the need for biliary drainage in a rural setting, answer her questions and safety-net.
focus: Jaundice with right upper quadrant pain and fever: recognising acute cholangitis (Charcot's triad), separating obstructive from hepatic jaundice and starting sepsis management with urgent biliary drainage
stem: You are a final-year medical student on your rural Emergency Department rotation. Marge Smith, a 28-year-old school teacher, has just been allocated to a bay. From a distance you notice that her skin looks obviously yellow. She has been triaged and has an IV cannula in with bloods sent. Your consultant has asked you to see her first. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Marge and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her blood results and venous gas, and an ultrasound report. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer the examiner's questions (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Marge Smith, a 28-year-old primary school teacher. You are Caucasian and not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. You are lying on the trolley holding your right upper tummy. You look flushed and sweaty and you are in a lot of pain, worse when each wave comes. You are worried but chatty between waves. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I have been getting the worst pain in my tummy, and my husband told me that my skin is looking a bit yellow..."

The pain (give only when asked)

  • Site: "On the right side, above my belly button." If asked to point, you point to the right upper quadrant, under the ribs.
  • Radiation: it does not go anywhere else.
  • Character: crampy. If asked: "It comes and goes in waves."
  • Severity: 8 out of 10. "I can't do much."
  • Onset and course: more sudden than gradual. It started about 2 hours ago at lunchtime and has been getting worse. You have never had anything like it before.
  • Better or worse: eating made it worse. Nothing relieves it, including opening your bowels.

The yellow skin (only when asked)

  • "I don't know, my husband just pointed it out before we came to hospital."
  • It has never happened before.
  • You have a mild itch all over (if asked to score it, 1 out of 4).

Other symptoms

Give these only to specific questions. If asked a vague "anything else?", say: "I'm not sure, like what?"

  • Fever: you have felt feverish, sweaty and had shivers (rigors). You have not taken your temperature. "The fevers, sweats and shivers started last night and have come and gone since; I felt washed out this morning. The bad pain only started at lunch."
  • Appetite: "The pain started while I was eating lunch and I couldn't finish it."
  • No change in weight.
  • Stools: pale and smelly over the last day or two.
  • Urine: dark over the last day or two. No blood in it.
  • No other change in your bowels. No nausea, vomiting, bloating or reflux.
  • No urinary symptoms (no burning, no frequency).
  • No chest pain, no shortness of breath, no palpitations.

Risk factors (only if asked about each)

  • No recent illness. No recent travel. No unusual food, takeaway or untreated water; nobody around you has been unwell.
  • No IV or recreational drugs ever. No tattoos or blood transfusions (if asked).
  • Alcohol: social only, a couple of glasses of wine on a weekend (if asked to quantify).
  • Sexual history: one partner, your husband. Safe sex: you use condoms and the pill.
  • You are not pregnant. You take the pill every day and have not missed any. If asked about your last period: it was normal, about 2 weeks ago.

Past history, medicines and allergies

  • Hayfever since childhood.
  • Appendix out at 13. No other operations on your tummy. You have never had a scan of your tummy.
  • No diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol or heart problems.
  • Medicines: Claratyne (loratadine) when you need it for hayfever. The combined oral contraceptive pill (oestrogen and progestogen) every day.
  • Allergies: shellfish, which gives you anaphylaxis. You carry an EpiPen. No allergies to any medicines.

Family history

  • Your mother had gallstones and had her gallbladder removed at 45.
  • Your father had lung cancer.

Social history

  • Primary school teacher. You live with your husband; no children. Fully independent.
  • Home-cooked meals. Pilates 3 times a week and the gym twice a week.
  • Smoking: 5 cigarettes a day since you were 18.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "Maybe something I ate? I really don't know why I'd be yellow."
  • Concern: you are frightened by the yellow skin and how unwell you feel, and worried it might be something serious with your liver.
  • Expectation: something for the pain, and to find out what is going on.
  • Question to raise once in Part 1: "Is it my liver? Is it serious?" A good candidate acknowledges the worry and explains they will know more once the tests are back.

The nurse and how Marge changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the triage set: RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 112/70, HR 112 regular, temperature 38.7 °C, alert, pain 8/10, BGL 5.8 mmol/L. Height 165 cm, weight 62 kg.
  • Partway through, the nurse says: "She's just started shaking uncontrollably, and she feels really hot."
  • If the candidate orders IV analgesia, the nurse gives it. A few minutes later Marge says the pain is about 4 out of 10 and she talks more easily. Without it she stays at 8 out of 10.
  • If the candidate orders blood cultures, antibiotics, fluids or anything else, the nurse confirms she will arrange it, and the examiner says: "Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2."
  • If asked for a urine dipstick: bilirubin 3+, urobilinogen negative, no blood, leucocytes or nitrites.
  • If asked about a pregnancy test: "A serum beta-hCG went with the triage bloods. The result will come with the others."
  • If the candidate asks for blood results or imaging, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: unwell, flushed and sweaty, in pain with each wave. Obviously jaundiced skin. A few faint scratch marks on the forearms. Alert and oriented to time, place and person; not confused.
  • Hydration: mucous membranes slightly dry. CRT 2 seconds, warm peripheries.
  • Eyes: yellow sclerae. No pallor.
  • Hands, face and chest wall: no palmar erythema, clubbing, leuconychia or spider naevi. No asterixis.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended. Healed right iliac fossa (appendicectomy) scar. No other scars, no visible mass.
  • Abdomen, palpation: tender in the right upper quadrant with mild voluntary guarding. No rebound tenderness and no rigidity. Murphy's sign negative. Gallbladder not palpable. Liver edge just palpable at the costal margin, smooth and tender; not enlarged. Spleen not palpable. No masses. Rest of the abdomen soft.
  • Percussion and auscultation: no shifting dullness. Bowel sounds present and normal.
  • Renal angles: not tender. Hernial orifices: normal.
  • Chest: equal expansion, resonant, clear breath sounds including the right base. Heart: dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Rectal or pelvic examination: if offered, the examiner says it is not needed.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Marge's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Acknowledges her 8/10 pain with empathy and asks the nurse for IV analgesia early, without waiting until the end of the history.

Uses plain language, explains each part of the examination before doing it, and responds to her worry that it is her liver by acknowledging it and saying the tests will help, without false reassurance.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: right upper quadrant, no radiation
Onset, course and severity: fairly sudden 2 hours ago, worsening, never before, 8/10
Modifying factors: worse with eating, nothing relieves it including opening her bowels

check.x: Characterises the jaundice: noticed by her husband today, never before, with a mild generalised itch.
Asks specifically about obstructive features and elicits pale, smelly stools and dark urine (no haematuria).
Asks specifically about fever and elicits feeling feverish with sweats and rigors since last night (temperature not taken).
Screens at least 3 other GI symptoms: appetite (couldn't finish lunch once the pain began), weight change, nausea or vomiting, other change in bowel habit, bloating, reflux.
Screens at least 2 other systems: urinary symptoms, chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations (all absent).
Asks about risk factors for hepatitis and other liver causes:

kids.x: IV or recreational drug use (none); credit tattoos or transfusions
Recent travel, recent illness, food and water exposure (none)
Sexual history (one partner, condoms and the pill)

check.x: Asks about the chance of pregnancy: contraception (OCP daily, condoms), last period and whether she could be pregnant (she is not).
Takes the past history: hayfever since childhood, appendicectomy at 13 and no other abdominal surgery, no previous imaging, no metabolic syndrome or cardiovascular risk factors.
Takes the medication history: Claratyne when needed and the combined oral contraceptive pill daily.
check.d: Credit noting the combined pill (oestrogen) as a gallstone risk factor.

check.x: Asks about allergies and the type of reaction: shellfish anaphylaxis, carries an EpiPen, no drug allergies.
Takes the family history and elicits her mother's gallstones with cholecystectomy at 45 (and her father's lung cancer).
Takes the social history: teacher, lives with husband, no children, independent, home-cooked meals, Pilates and gym, smokes 5 a day since 18.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause, frightened it is her liver, wants pain relief and an answer.
Examination
Asks for the full set of vital signs, identifies the fever (38.7 °C) and tachycardia (HR 112), and with the rigors tells the nurse or consultant early that she may be septic.
check.d: Credit asking for blood cultures and a lactate in Part 1.

check.x: General inspection: jaundiced skin and sclerae, flushed and sweaty, scratch marks; checks her mental state (alert and oriented, not confused).
check.d: The critical element is checking for confusion.

check.x: Assesses hydration and perfusion: slightly dry mucous membranes, CRT 2 seconds, warm peripheries.
Looks for stigmata of chronic liver disease and asterixis (none).
Inspects the abdomen: not distended, appendicectomy scar.
Palpates gently starting away from the pain: right upper quadrant tenderness with mild guarding, no rebound or rigidity, Murphy's sign negative.
Palpates the liver edge (just palpable, tender, smooth), the gallbladder (not palpable), the spleen and for masses.
Examines the chest including the right base, the heart and the renal angles.
Asks for a urine dipstick (bilirubin 3+, urobilinogen negative).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: temperature 38.7 then 39.1 °C in the yellow zone at both sets; at 14:40 HR 124 and SBP 98 have moved into the yellow zone with rigors. She is deteriorating and needs an immediate clinical review, with a rapid response if any value enters the red zone. Credit a rapid response call for multiple yellow-zone observations with staff concern, as per local CERS.
Interprets the WCC of 17.8 with neutrophilia and the CRP of 186 as a marked inflammatory response in keeping with bacterial infection.
Interprets the LFTs as cholestatic: conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (bilirubin 68) with ALP 296 and GGT 384 raised more than the transaminases, pointing to post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice.
check.d: Credit noting that an early transaminase rise is common when a duct stone first obstructs.

check.x: States that the serum beta-hCG is negative (not pregnant), and that a normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely.

Interprets the lactate of 2.6 as raised: suspected sepsis on the SEPSIS KILLS pathway (infection plus yellow-zone observations), with lactate 2.6 showing early hypoperfusion; notes normal creatinine, INR and platelets with no confusion: no other organ dysfunction yet.
Interprets the ultrasound: dilated common bile duct (11 mm) with a stone in the distal duct, mild intrahepatic duct dilatation, gallstones, and no features of acute cholecystitis.

Gives acute (ascending) cholangitis from a common bile duct stone as the most likely diagnosis, justified by Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever with rigors, jaundice), the obstructive features, the cholestatic LFTs and the dilated duct with a stone.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: TG18 definite diagnosis, moderate (Grade II) because WCC is above 12 and temperature is 39 °C or more.

check.x: Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: acute cholecystitis, acute viral hepatitis, gallstone pancreatitis, pancreatic or periampullary malignancy, bowel obstruction.
Management

Treats as sepsis: ABCDE, blood cultures before antibiotics, then IV antibiotics within 60 minutes per eTG: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV (about 430 mg for 62 kg) as a single dose, then the interval by renal function; or piperacillin+tazobactam 4+0.5 g IV 6-hourly; ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily if gentamicin is contraindicated.
check.d: Credit any correct eTG regimen; the critical elements are cultures before antibiotics and IV antibiotics without delay.

check.x: Gives 500 mL IV crystalloid (Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride) over 15 to 30 minutes, reassesses, and repeats to response up to about 20 to 30 mL/kg (about 1.2 to 1.8 L), then maintenance; IDC or strict fluid balance chart with a urine output target of at least 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 30 mL/h).
check.d: The critical element is an IV crystalloid bolus with reassessment of response; credit the volumes and urine-output target but do not require them.

check.x: Gives titrated IV opioid analgesia, keeps her nil by mouth for a procedure, and repeats the lactate after resuscitation.

Escalates to the consultant and refers to the general surgical or gastroenterology team at the referral hospital for transfer and biliary drainage by ERCP (early, within about 24 to 48 hours; urgently if she does not respond to fluids and antibiotics), with ICU and retrieval involvement if she becomes shocked.
Plans a cholecystectomy during the same admission once the cholangitis has settled, to prevent recurrence.
Safety netting

Asks the nurse for at least hourly observations and to escalate at least 3 of: falling BP, rising HR, new confusion or drowsiness, urine output below target, rising lactate, worsening pain; rapid response for any red-zone value.

Explains to Marge in plain words that a gallstone has slipped into and blocked the bile duct and the bile behind it is infected; she needs antibiotics, fluids and a transfer for a camera procedure to clear the duct; tells her to call the nurse at once for worse pain, more shaking, feeling faint or confused.
Answers Marge's question about her shellfish allergy: it is not a reason to avoid iodinated contrast at ERCP; the anaphylaxis is still documented and her EpiPen kept with her.

part2.lead: Here are Marge's observations, her blood results and venous gas, and the ultrasound report.
part2.patient: While the candidate answers, ask once: "The nurse said something about dye for the procedure. I'm allergic to shellfish. Is that a problem?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air. Triage set at 14:15 and the nurse's repeat set at 14:40, taken during a further episode of rigors. No urine passed since arrival.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: the 14:40 pain score is blank. If IV analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate it is 4/10 after IV analgesia; otherwise tell them it is 8/10 and no analgesia has been given. The 14:40 set was taken before any fluid ordered in Part 1 had run in. If cultures and antibiotics were ordered in Part 1, they were given at 14:45, before the ultrasound. If not, they are now overdue: credit a candidate who says so and gives them immediately, without waiting for further imaging.
  • Read: at 14:15, temperature 38.7 °C is in the yellow zone; HR 112, BP 112/70, RR 18 and SpO2 98% on room air are white. At 14:40, temperature 39.1 °C (yellow), HR 124 (yellow) and SBP 98 (yellow), CRT 3 seconds, rigors, nurse concerned; RR and SpO2 white, alert.
  • Meaning: a febrile, rigoring patient whose heart rate is rising and blood pressure falling: sepsis that is getting worse, heading towards septic shock. Nothing is in the red zone yet.
  • Changes: several yellow-zone values with nurse concern call for an immediate clinical review (this review) and senior involvement. She needs cultures, antibiotics and fluids now, and observations at least hourly. Call a rapid response if any value enters the red zone (for example SBP below 90).

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: RUQ pain, jaundiced, febrile. IV cannula, bloods sent
Repeat set during rigors. No urine passed. Pain score: see examiner

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Collected 14:20 at cannulation; venous gas on room air at the same time. Sample not haemolysed. No previous results on file. Hepatitis serology to follow from the regional laboratory.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 17.8 with neutrophils 15.2, CRP 186. Bilirubin 68, mostly conjugated (54). ALP 296 and GGT 384 raised more than ALT 182 and AST 141. Albumin, INR, platelets, creatinine and electrolytes normal. Lipase 42 normal. Beta-hCG below 2. Venous gas: pH 7.36, bicarbonate 23, lactate 2.6 (raised). Hepatitis serology pending.
  • Meaning: marked inflammation with a cholestatic, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia: post-hepatic obstruction with infection. The ALT rise is common early in duct obstruction and does not mean hepatitis. Normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely. Not pregnant. Suspected sepsis on the SEPSIS KILLS pathway (infection plus yellow-zone observations); lactate 2.6 shows early hypoperfusion; normal creatinine, INR and platelets with a clear mind mean no other organ dysfunction yet. TG18: WCC above 12 plus fever of 39 °C or more makes this moderate (Grade II).
  • Changes: sepsis treatment now; normal renal function allows gentamicin; repeat lactate after fluids; follow up serology.

labs.title: Liver function tests, lipase and coagulation

rows.t: Hepatitis A IgM, HBsAg, HCV antibody

handover.label: Ultrasound of the upper abdomen
handover.result:
Examination: ultrasound of the upper abdomen (liver, gallbladder, biliary tree, pancreas, right kidney), 15:00.

Clinical details: 28-year-old woman, fevers since last night, RUQ pain for 2 hours, jaundice, fever 39.1 °C with rigors, pale stools and dark urine. Bilirubin 68, ALP 296, GGT 384, WCC 17.8. Beta-hCG negative. ?Biliary obstruction ?Cholangitis.

Findings:

  • Gallbladder: normal size. Multiple mobile echogenic calculi up to 8 mm with posterior acoustic shadowing. Wall 2 mm, not thickened. No pericholecystic fluid. Sonographic Murphy's sign negative.
  • Bile ducts: common bile duct dilated to 11 mm. A 9 mm echogenic shadowing calculus in the distal common bile duct. Mild intrahepatic duct dilatation in both lobes.
  • Liver: normal size and echotexture. No focal lesion. No abscess.
  • Pancreas: head partly obscured by bowel gas; the visualised head, body and tail are normal in size and echotexture. No mass seen and no peripancreatic fluid. Pancreatic duct not dilated.
  • Right kidney: normal, no hydronephrosis.
  • Other: no free fluid. No right pleural effusion.

Conclusion: choledocholithiasis with a distal common bile duct stone and intra- and extrahepatic biliary dilatation. Cholelithiasis without features of acute cholecystitis. Clinical correlation for cholangitis is advised.
handover.model:
• Read: CBD 11 mm (normally up to about 6 mm) with a 9 mm distal duct stone, mild intrahepatic dilatation, multiple gallstones, thin gallbladder wall, no pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's negative. Liver normal, no abscess. Pancreas normal where seen. No free fluid.
  • Meaning: a stone has passed from the gallbladder into the common bile duct and is blocking it. With fever, rigors and jaundice this is acute cholangitis, a TG18 definite diagnosis (inflammation, cholestasis and imaging). No cholecystitis. No mass seen, though the pancreatic head is partly obscured; a stone explains the picture in a 28-year-old.
  • Changes: she needs biliary drainage by ERCP to remove the stone, which is not available here, so she needs transfer. Cholecystectomy follows later in the same admission. MRCP is not needed when the stone is already seen.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar at the regional referral hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Marge Smith, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Marge now, here in the emergency department.
Marge asks you, "What's wrong with me, and what happens now?" Please answer her, then tell me what you would ask the nurses to watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year student in the rural ED (with consultant); Marge Smith, 28.
  • Situation: acute cholangitis from a common bile duct stone, septic and deteriorating; requesting transfer for ERCP.
  • Background: fevers with sweats and rigors since last night, then 2 hours of crampy RUQ pain; jaundice, pale stools, dark urine, itch; on the combined OCP, mother had gallstones; shellfish anaphylaxis, no drug allergies; not pregnant.
  • Assessment: T 39.1 °C, HR 112 rising to 124, SBP 98 (yellow zone), alert; WCC 17.8, CRP 186; cholestatic LFTs, bilirubin 68; lipase normal; lactate 2.6; creatinine and INR normal; ultrasound: CBD 11 mm with a distal stone, gallstones, no cholecystitis.
  • Recommendation: cultures, antibiotics and fluids started or being started; please accept for transfer and early ERCP; advise if you want anything more before transfer.

Acute cholangitis from choledocholithiasis: Charcot's triad (RUQ pain, fever with rigors, jaundice), pale stools, dark urine, itch, cholestatic LFTs, raised WCC and CRP, dilated CBD with a stone; risk factors female, fertile, fair, OCP, mother with gallstones.

  • Acute cholecystitis: for: risk factors, RUQ pain, fever; against: jaundice, Murphy's negative, normal gallbladder wall.
  • Acute viral hepatitis: for: jaundice, ALT 182; against: no risk factors, cholestatic pattern, dilated duct.
  • Gallstone pancreatitis: for: duct stone; against: lipase 42, normal pancreas.
  • Pancreatic or periampullary malignancy: for: obstructive jaundice; against: age 28, acute painful onset, no weight loss, stone seen.
  • Bowel obstruction: for: colicky pain, appendicectomy; against: no vomiting or distension, bowels open.

1. ABCDE and sepsis pathway; senior (consultant) at the bedside.
  2. Blood cultures, then IV antibiotics within 60 minutes per eTG: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV (about 430 mg for 62 kg) as a single dose, then the interval by renal function; or piperacillin+tazobactam 4+0.5 g IV 6-hourly; ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily if gentamicin is contraindicated.
  3. Fluids: 500 mL IV crystalloid (Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride) over 15 to 30 minutes, reassess, repeat to response up to about 20 to 30 mL/kg (about 1.2 to 1.8 L); IDC or fluid balance, urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; repeat lactate.
  4. Titrated IV opioid; nil by mouth.
  5. Refer and transfer to a centre with ERCP for early biliary drainage (urgent if not responding); ICU and retrieval if shocked.
  6. Cholecystectomy in the same admission once settled.

• Plain words: a gallstone has moved into the tube that drains bile from the liver and blocked it; the trapped bile is infected, which is why she is yellow, feverish and shaking. It is serious but treatable.
  • What happens now: a drip, antibiotics and pain relief, then transfer to the bigger hospital for a camera test through the mouth to clear the duct; the gallbladder is usually removed later in the same stay. Shellfish allergy is not a reason to avoid the dye.
  • Call the nurse at once for worse pain, more shaking, feeling faint or muddled.
  • Nurses: hourly observations; escalate falling BP, rising HR or new confusion; rapid response for any red-zone value.

ddx.for: RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad), pale stools, dark urine and itch, cholestatic LFTs with WCC 17.8 and CRP 186, and an 11 mm common bile duct with a distal stone.
Female, 28, on the OCP, mother with gallstones, RUQ pain worse with food and fever, gallstones on ultrasound.
ddx.against: She is jaundiced with obstructive features, Murphy's sign is negative, and the gallbladder wall is thin with no pericholecystic fluid.

ddx.for: Jaundice with a tender liver edge and an ALT of 182.
ddx.against: No IV drugs, travel or unsafe sex, the LFTs are cholestatic with ALP and GGT raised more than ALT, and the bile ducts are dilated.

ddx.for: A stone in the distal common bile duct with severe upper abdominal pain.
ddx.against: Lipase 42 is normal, the pain does not go through to the back, and the visualised pancreas is normal.

ddx.for: Obstructive jaundice with pale stools and dark urine, a smoker, and the pancreatic head partly obscured on ultrasound.
ddx.against: She is 28, the onset is acute and painful, there is no weight loss, the gallbladder is not palpable and a duct stone explains the obstruction.

ddx.for: Crampy pain in waves after a previous appendicectomy.
ddx.against: No vomiting, distension or change in bowel habit, normal bowel sounds, and the ultrasound shows a biliary cause.

guide:
In Part 1, Marge gives each detail only when asked. She gives the associated symptoms only to specific questions; to a vague "anything else?" she says "I'm not sure, like what?". The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The nurse reports the rigors partway through. If the candidate orders cultures, antibiotics or fluids in Part 1, say "Noted, please cover it in Part 2" and credit early recognition of sepsis (item 21). If they ask for results or imaging, say these come in Part 2.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, the bloods and gas, and the ultrasound report, then ask all four questions in order. The 14:40 pain score is blank: give 4/10 if IV analgesia was ordered in Part 1, otherwise 8/10 with no analgesia given. Read Marge's question to open question 4; while the candidate answers, she asks once about her shellfish allergy and the dye.

A high-performing candidate asks specifically about fever, stools, urine and itch, screens the hepatitis risk factors and pregnancy, and records the shellfish anaphylaxis. They notice the fever and tachycardia early and say she may be septic, and they check for confusion and Murphy's sign. In Part 2 they name Charcot's triad, read the LFTs as obstructive and the ultrasound as a duct stone, and see that she is deteriorating. They give cultures and IV antibiotics within the hour, give fluids, and arrange transfer for ERCP.

A borderline candidate takes a pain history but misses the fever or the stool and urine colour, calls it cholecystitis or hepatitis, or plans ERCP without antibiotics and fluids. A failing candidate misses the sepsis, or plans discharge or an outpatient scan.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute cholangitis from a common bile duct stone

Marge has Charcot's triad: right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and jaundice. Pale stools, dark urine and itch show that bile is not reaching the bowel and conjugated bilirubin is spilling into the blood and urine, so the jaundice is post-hepatic (obstructive). She has no risk factors for viral hepatitis. She has the classic gallstone risk factors: female, fair, fertile, oestrogen (the combined pill) and a mother who had a cholecystectomy at 45. A stone has passed from the gallbladder into the common bile duct, blocked it, and the bile behind it has become infected. Cholangitis can progress to septic shock within hours. Adding confusion and hypotension to the triad gives Reynolds' pentad, which marks severe disease.

Approach: classify the jaundice

  • Pre-hepatic: haemolysis. Unconjugated bilirubin, normal-coloured urine and stools (Gilbert syndrome, a hepatic conjugation defect, gives the same pattern).
  • Hepatic: viral, alcohol-related, drug-induced or autoimmune hepatitis. Transaminases raised more than ALP.
  • Post-hepatic: duct stones, strictures, pancreatic or periampullary cancer. Pale stools, dark urine, itch, ALP and GGT raised more than transaminases, dilated ducts on ultrasound.

Then screen the risk factors for each organ in the right upper quadrant: gallstones (female, fair, fat, forty, fertile, family history), hepatitis B and C (unprotected sex, IV drugs, tattoos), hepatitis A and parasites (travel, food and water), and alcohol (hepatitis, pancreatitis). In any woman of reproductive age, ask about pregnancy: pregnancy changes imaging, drugs and procedures, and has its own causes of jaundice and RUQ pain.

Diagnostic criteria and severity (Tokyo Guidelines 2018)

TG18 makes a definite diagnosis with all three of:

  • systemic inflammation (fever or shaking chills, raised WCC or CRP);
  • cholestasis (jaundice, abnormal LFTs);
  • imaging (biliary dilatation or a cause such as a stone).

Marge meets all three. Grade III (severe) means organ dysfunction: hypotension needing vasopressors, confusion, respiratory failure, renal impairment, INR above 1.5 or platelets below 100. Grade II (moderate) needs two of: WCC above 12 or below 4, fever of 39 °C or more, age 75 or more, bilirubin of 85 µmol/L (5 mg/dL) or more, low albumin. Otherwise it is Grade I (mild). Marge is Grade II (WCC 17.8 and fever 39.1 °C), but her falling blood pressure means she could become Grade III if she does not respond to fluids.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: fever in the yellow zone at both sets, then HR and SBP moving into the yellow zone with rigors. She is deteriorating and needs an immediate clinical review; a red-zone value means a rapid response.
  • Bloods: raised WCC and CRP. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with ALP and GGT raised more than the transaminases is cholestatic. Transaminases often rise sharply in the first hours of duct obstruction and can mislead towards hepatitis. Normal lipase makes pancreatitis unlikely; negative beta-hCG excludes pregnancy. This is suspected sepsis on the SEPSIS KILLS pathway (infection plus yellow-zone observations); lactate 2.6 shows early hypoperfusion; normal creatinine, INR and platelets mean no other organ dysfunction yet.
  • Ultrasound: a dilated duct with a distal stone and gallstones. A thin gallbladder wall and negative sonographic Murphy's sign mean no cholecystitis.

Management

  • Sepsis: ABCDE, early senior involvement, blood cultures, then IV antibiotics within 60 minutes as the NSW SEPSIS KILLS pathway sets out. eTG options: amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV (about 430 mg for 62 kg) as a single dose, then the interval by renal function; or piperacillin+tazobactam 4+0.5 g IV 6-hourly; ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily if gentamicin is contraindicated. Give 500 mL IV crystalloid (Hartmann's or 0.9% sodium chloride) over 15 to 30 minutes, reassess, and repeat to response up to about 20 to 30 mL/kg (about 1.2 to 1.8 L), then repeat the lactate. Use an IDC or fluid balance chart.
  • Analgesia: titrated IV opioid; nil by mouth before a procedure.
  • Source control: antibiotics alone do not clear an obstructed, infected duct. TG18 advises early biliary drainage for Grade II and urgent drainage, once resuscitated, for Grade III or failure to respond. ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction (or a stent) is first-line. Most rural hospitals cannot do ERCP, so Marge needs early referral and transfer, with retrieval and ICU involvement if she becomes shocked.
  • Prevent recurrence: cholecystectomy during the same admission once the cholangitis has settled.
  • Allergy: shellfish allergy does not predict a reaction to iodinated contrast and is not a reason to withhold contrast. Her anaphylaxis is still documented.
  • Admission care: VTE risk assessment (the combined pill, surgery), and follow-up of hepatitis serology. Withhold the combined oral contraceptive pill (and advise alternative contraception) and give VTE prophylaxis per local protocol once bleeding risk around ERCP is considered.

Differentials

Acute cholecystitis gives RUQ pain and fever with a positive Murphy's sign; marked jaundice and a dilated duct are unusual in cholecystitis and suggest a duct stone (or Mirizzi syndrome). Acute hepatitis gives jaundice with transaminases far above ALP and normal ducts. Pancreatitis is diagnosed by 2 of 3: typical pain, lipase more than 3 times the upper limit, or imaging features; a normal lipase makes it unlikely. Pancreatic or periampullary cancer classically gives painless jaundice with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law). Bowel obstruction gives colic with vomiting, distension and constipation.

Safety netting

Nurses observe her at least hourly and escalate a falling BP, rising HR, confusion, low urine output or rising lactate, calling a rapid response for any red-zone value. Marge calls the nurse for worse pain, more shaking, faintness or confusion. After discharge she sees her GP for repeat LFTs, the operation plan and smoking cessation. If her cholecystectomy is deferred, she returns to the ED for fever, jaundice or pain while she waits.
points: RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad) is acute cholangitis until proven otherwise. Confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) mean severe disease.
Classify jaundice as pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic. Pale stools, dark urine, itch and ALP and GGT raised more than transaminases point to obstruction; always ask about each one specifically.
Screen the risk factors for each RUQ organ: gallstones (female, fair, fertile, OCP, family history), viral hepatitis (IV drugs, sex, travel) and alcohol. Always ask about pregnancy.

Ultrasound is the first test: a dilated common bile duct, with or without a visible stone, confirms obstruction. TG18 grades severity by organ dysfunction (Grade III); Grade II needs two of: WCC above 12 or below 4, fever of 39 °C or more, age 75 or more, bilirubin of 85 µmol/L or more, low albumin.

Treat as sepsis: blood cultures, IV antibiotics within 60 minutes per eTG, fluids and lactate, then early biliary drainage by ERCP (urgent if not responding). In a rural ED this means early referral and transfer.
Shellfish allergy is not a contraindication to iodinated contrast. Cholecystectomy in the same admission prevents recurrence.
